issues.legal_issue: A bona fide association or member of the public may invoke judicial review on behalf of a disadvantaged group affected by state action.
material_facts: The association represented the interests of slum dwellers affected by the government’s notification.
One appellant was a resident of the area.
The challenge concerned action affecting a class of persons, some of whom were socially or economically disadvantaged.
issues.conclusion: The appellants had standing to invoke the Court’s jurisdiction, and the High Court was wrong to hold otherwise.
issues.legal_principle: A bona fide member of the public may seek enforcement of fundamental rights for people who cannot approach the court because of poverty, disability, or social or economic disadvantage. The Court relied on Bandhua Mukti Morcha v. Union of India and referred to S. P. Gupta v. Union of India and Olga Tellis v. Bombay Municipal Corporation.

predicates.public_interest_challenge_to_state_actio: The proceeding seeks judicial review of state action on behalf of an affected group.
predicates.bona_fide_representative_of_affected_gro: A bona fide association represents the interests of the group affected by the state action.
predicates.member_of_affected_group: The person bringing the proceeding belongs to the group affected by the state action.
predicates.disadvantaged_group_cannot_readily_appro: The group is unable to approach the court readily because of poverty, disability, or social or economic disadvantage.

issues.definition: When a public-interest challenge concerns state action affecting a disadvantaged group that cannot readily approach the court, a bona fide representative or group member has standing.

issues.legal_issue: The power to issue a statutory notification includes the power to rescind it, subject to the same manner, sanctions, and conditions that govern its issue.
material_facts: The government had issued notifications under the slum legislation declaring an area to be a slum area and then a slum clearance area.
The government later issued a notification cancelling the earlier notification and declaring a smaller area.
The appellants argued that the legislation did not specifically authorize rescission.
issues.conclusion: The government had power to rescind the earlier notification under the applicable General Clauses Act provision, but that power remained subject to the conditions governing its exercise.
issues.legal_principle: Section 21 of the General Clauses Act, 1897, which is in pari materia with section 10 of the Karnataka General Clauses Act, 1899, provides that a power to issue a notification includes power to amend, vary, or rescind it, exercisable in the like manner and subject to like sanctions and conditions. The Court relied on State of Kerala v. K. G. Madhavan Pillai, State of M.P. v. V. P. Sharma, Lt. Governor of H.P. v. Sri Avinash Sharma, Lachmi Narain v. Union of India, State of Bihar v. D. N. Ganguly, and Kamla Prasad Khetan v. Union of India.

predicates.administrative_notification_issued_under: An authority issued a notification under a statutory power.
predicates.no_inconsistent_statutory_provision: The statute’s subject matter, context, and effect do not make an implied power of rescission inconsistent with its provisions.

issues.definition: When an authority issued a statutory notification and the statute does not preclude rescission, the authority may rescind it subject to the conditions governing its issue.

issues.legal_issue: An authority must give affected inhabitants an opportunity to be heard before rescinding or altering prior slum-area declarations in a way that prejudicially affects them.
material_facts: The government had first declared a larger area to be a slum area and then declared it a slum clearance area after considering objections.
The government later cancelled the earlier notification and declared only a smaller area, excluding much of the previously covered area.
Inhabitants had been affected by the earlier action and the change affected the scope of the scheme concerning their area.
The affected slum dwellers were not given an opportunity to be heard before the change.
issues.conclusion: Rescinding the earlier notifications without hearing the affected slum dwellers violated natural justice, so the later notification was quashed; the government could proceed after giving them an opportunity to be heard.
issues.legal_principle: The audi alteram partem rule applies when the statutory duty and circumstances imply an obligation to hear, unless the statute prohibits a hearing. Where the exercise of power can prejudice a person, a duty to act judicially is implicit. Sections 3 and 11 of the Karnataka Slum Areas (Improvement and Clearance) Act, 1973, including the proviso to section 11(1), and the Act’s purpose of improving public health informed the requirement to hear inhabitants affected by alteration of the scheme. The Court relied on Government of Mysore v. J. V. Bhat and applied the requirement that rescission under section 21 of the General Clauses Act, 1897, be exercised subject to like conditions.

predicates.administrative_change_to_existing_slum_a: An authority rescinds or alters an earlier declaration or scheme concerning a slum area.
predicates.affected_inhabitants_prejudiced_by_chang: The change affects inhabitants who were affected by the authority’s earlier action concerning the area.
predicates.affected_inhabitants_heard: The authority gave the affected inhabitants an opportunity to be heard before making the change.

issues.definition: When an authority changes an existing slum-area scheme in a way that prejudices affected inhabitants, the change is invalid if they were not heard first.
